title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 335
paragraphs: Thus the priests of the Egyptians told me; and I myself agree with the story told about Helen, adding this consideration: if Helen had been in Ilion, she would have been given up to the Hellenes, whether Alexander consented or no. For assuredly Priam was not so mad, nor the others of his house, as to be willing to run the risk of ruin for themselves, their children, and their city, in order that Alexander might have Helen as his wife. And even supposing that for the first part of the time they had been so inclined, yet when many other Trojans besides were losing their lives as often as they fought with the Hellenes, and when of Priam's own sons two or three or even more were slain in every battle (if one may trust at all the Epic poets) — when, I say, things were coming to such a pass, I believe that even if Priam himself had had Helen as wife, he would have given her back to the Achaeans, if by so doing he might be freed from the evils that oppressed him. Nor was the kingdom coming to Alexander next, so that with Priam old the government was in his hands; but Hector, who was both older and more of a man than he, would have received it after Priam's death, and it would not have befitted Hector to allow his brother to continue his wrongdoing, seeing that great evils were coming to pass on his account both to himself privately and in general to the other Trojans. In truth, however, they lacked the power to give Helen back; and the Hellenes did not believe them, though they spoke the truth — because, as I declare my opinion, the divine power was purposing to cause them utterly to perish, and so make it evident to men that for great wrongs great also are the chastisements that come from the gods. And thus have I delivered my opinion concerning these matters.
